content.content:
=== claim--thigh-angular-velocity-and-sprint-speed
# Faster Sprinters Swing the Thigh Faster ("Whip From the Hip")
**What it is** — Moyer cites Ken Clark's work to support his "switching" observation: across subjects and trials in Clark's "whip from the hip" study, **thigh angular velocity showed a strong positive linear correlation with running speed** and with lower-limb vertical velocity at touchdown. He adds Clark's later work on **horizontal foot speed** (the foot moving backward relative to the body before contact, sometimes called negative foot speed, measured with shoe-mounted inertial sensors) and Peter Weyand's summary that the fastest sprinters "cock the knee high before driving the foot into the ground while maintaining a stiff ankle". His own addition, made in the live session: **"you can't whip if the thigh doesn't go high"** — pawback speed depends on how high knee drive took the thigh first.
**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: a faster swing brings the foot down and back at higher speed, so the foot lands closer under the centre of mass (less braking) and the lower limb strikes the ground harder, which supports the large, brief vertical forces fast running needs (Clark and Weyand's two-mass model). The research relationship is **correlational and cross-sectional** — faster runners swing faster. It does not show that training thigh speed makes an athlete faster. Moyer also says, lovingly, that Clark "regurgitates" what 1980s Soviet reports already found; that is his opinion about priority, not a finding.
**When to apply** — As the evidence base for watching switching on film; as a reason to include hip-flexor and swing-speed work in a speed block; when reading GPS max velocity next to film (an athlete whose top speed stalls often shows a low thigh in front and slow retraction).
**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, not higher: the citations were read aloud on slides and were not checked against the papers in this ingest. Correlation across a speed range partly reflects the fact that running faster *requires* a faster limb swing — it is close to a description of speed rather than a separate cause of it. Do not coach "paw back" as a cue in isolation: the live session records the common failure where athletes cast the foot out in front and pull it back, which lands the foot ahead of the hips. Moyer says he teaches pawback only when needed, and always with the foot landing as close under the body as possible.
**Example** — Two receivers top out at 9.1 m/s on GPS. On side film one shows a high thigh and fast retraction; the other's thigh barely passes horizontal and the foot drops straight down. The second athlete is the candidate for knee-drive and retraction work, and his next GPS top speed is the check.
**Related** — [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]] — the same thigh action is what Moyer says fails first under fatigue.
=== claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver
# The Ankle Plantar Flexors as the Main "Driving Link" at Top Speed
**What it is** — Moyer's case that the foot and ankle, not the knee, drive the push-off at maximal speed. He strings together figures from several sources:
- Soleus and gastrocnemius generate **77% of vertical and 60% of horizontal** centre-of-mass acceleration; the soleus gives vertical support at all speeds, the gastrocnemius more horizontal propulsion.
- The Achilles tendon "accumulates **75–90%** of the mechanical energy" (source not named).
- From a 1981 *Soviet Sports Review* article out of Zatsiorsky's lab: during takeoff external energy rises by **340 J**; knee muscles do **31 J**, plantar flexors **192 J** ("more than six times as much"), so "the main driving link in running with maximum sustained speed is the foot". The foot-ankle returns **60–70%** of the landing energy.
- Push-off "can generate up to **20%** of the force" in sprinting (attributed to Yessis; Moyer says in the live session he does not know where that figure came from).
**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: the foot and ankle work eccentrically then concentrically in each contact, storing energy in the tendon as the body passes over the foot and giving it back at push-off. The training conclusion he draws is to develop the "spring-like properties of the foot, calves and tendons" — calf strength, ankle plyometrics, foot work.
**When to apply** — As a reason to keep calf, Achilles and foot work in a speed programme (single-leg calf raises, ankle-dominant plyometrics, isometrics), and to look at the ankle when an athlete sinks at contact.
**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: these are force- and energy-share figures quoted from slides, mixing different measures (muscle contribution to acceleration, tendon energy storage, joint work) from different studies and different speeds, none checked in this ingest. They cannot be added together, and "20% of the force" sits awkwardly next to "192 of 340 J". The 77%/60% figure resembles musculoskeletal-modelling results (e.g. Dorn, Schache and Pandy's running simulations), which are model outputs, not measurements. Joint-work studies of maximal sprinting generally find the **hip** dominates at the highest speeds, with the ankle's share plateauing — so "the foot is the main driver" should not be repeated as settled. The practical advice (train the calf-Achilles complex) does not depend on these numbers being right.
**Example** — A running back's contact looks soft on film and his ankle collapses. Moyer's framework says train the calf-Achilles spring; a sound version of that is to add single-leg calf strength and ankle hops and re-film, without citing "the Achilles does 90% of the work" to the athlete.
**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — ankle extension is the third local key action. The knee-extension-at-toe-off argument that Moyer builds on these figures (knee should not exceed ~165°) is covered in a separate, contested entry.
=== framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles
# Four Acceleration Profiles (After J. J. Wild) as a Starting Point for Training
**What it is** — Moyer uses J. J. Wild's research (introduced to him by Jonas Dodoo's Speedworks group) that sorts team-sport athletes' early-acceleration strategies into four groups from step length, step rate, contact time and flight time. His labels and descriptions:
1. **Bounders — step length + air-based.** Long strides and good projection, but they pop up vertically; hips rise too early.
2. **Drivers — step length + ground-based.** Long strides and good projection, but very little air time; hips stay low with no rise; "mushy", not bouncy.
3. **Spinners — step frequency + ground-based.** Quick steps that "spin the wheels"; the foot barely leaves the ground.
4. **Bouncers — step frequency + air-based.** Quick steps but bouncing up and down; looks like jumping. He also calls this the "Fred Flintstone" runner (he uses that label loosely elsewhere).
His training response is to **move each athlete toward the middle**, not into a best quadrant: bounders a little more ground-based (more force into the ground, especially in acceleration); drivers a little more bouncy; spinners better projection plus a bit more bounce; bouncers better projection and more force. Live-session examples: for **bounders**, ankle range work, heavy sleds, single-leg calf raises, pawback work (banded marches, banded bounding); for **drivers**, foot isometrics, squats with a pause, pawbacks, and extensive jumps for stiffness.
**Why it works** — Categorising reduces complexity (he quotes Stu McMillan): in a squad of 20–40, four buckets let you individualise the first 10–15 minutes of a session with four or five group-specific exercises while the rest of the plan stays common.
**When to apply** — Group individualisation in team speed sessions; a first-pass sort after camp testing, using side-on film of the first 10 yd (plus timing gates or GPS acceleration data if available).
**When NOT to apply** — Wild's categories come from measured kinematics; Moyer's use is a **qualitative, by-eye sort**, with no reliability data and no reported evidence that bucket-specific training beats common training. The four labels (bounders etc.) may be Moyer's or Speedworks' shorthand rather than Wild's — check before citing. His training response per bucket is his own opinion; responses for spinners and bouncers were stated only in outline. A profile is a strategy, not a fault — strong defensive linemen may be "drivers" for good reasons over 5 yd. Do not use the bucket to predict injury (see [[claim--acceleration-profile-predicts-injury-site]]).
**Example** — Of 16 skill players, four are bounders. In the first 12 minutes of speed day they do heavy sled marches and single-leg calf raises while the drivers do pogo series and pawback drills; everyone then runs the common acceleration session.
**Related** — [[principle--individualization]] (periodization--bompa) — agreement: individualise where capacities genuinely diverge; buckets are a cheap middle ground.
=== claim--acceleration-profile-predicts-injury-site
# Acceleration Profile Linked to Injury Site
**What it is** — As Moyer reports it, J. J. Wild also looked for injury patterns across the four acceleration profiles (one study shown was in female team-sport athletes) and found them:
- **Quadrant 1 (bounders — length, air):** calf, Achilles and foot.
- **Quadrant 2 (drivers — length, ground):** patella and quad; hip and thigh.
- **Quadrant 3 (spinners — frequency, ground):** hip flexors and adductors.
- **Quadrant 4 (bouncers — frequency, air):** calf, Achilles, foot and hip flexors — the widest spread of soft-tissue injuries.
He summarises that "sprint acceleration strategies can be linked to specific injury sites", with examples such as poor hamstring engagement in acceleration causing hamstring strains and excessive braking in the first steps straining the calf.
**Why it works** — Asserted: each strategy loads different tissues more heavily (e.g. more braking in the first steps loads the calf). That is plausible but not demonstrated here.

=== claim--thigh-angular-velocity-and-sprint-speed
# Faster Sprinters Swing the Thigh Faster ("Whip From the Hip")
**What it is** — Moyer cites Ken Clark's work to support his "switching" observation: across subjects and trials in Clark's "whip from the hip" study, **thigh angular velocity showed a strong positive linear correlation with running speed** and with lower-limb vertical velocity at touchdown. He adds Clark's later work on **horizontal foot speed** (the foot moving backward relative to the body before contact, sometimes called negative foot speed, measured with shoe-mounted inertial sensors) and Peter Weyand's summary that the fastest sprinters "cock the knee high before driving the foot into the ground while maintaining a stiff ankle". His own addition, made in the live session: **"you can't whip if the thigh doesn't go high"** — pawback speed depends on how high knee drive took the thigh first.
**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: a faster swing brings the foot down and back at higher speed, so the foot lands closer under the centre of mass (less braking) and the lower limb strikes the ground harder, which supports the large, brief vertical forces fast running needs (Clark and Weyand's two-mass model). The research relationship is **correlational and cross-sectional** — faster runners swing faster. It does not show that training thigh speed makes an athlete faster. Moyer also says, lovingly, that Clark "regurgitates" what 1980s Soviet reports already found; that is his opinion about priority, not a finding.
**When to apply** — As the evidence base for watching switching on film; as a reason to include hip-flexor and swing-speed work in a speed block; when reading GPS max velocity next to film (an athlete whose top speed stalls often shows a low thigh in front and slow retraction).
**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, not higher: the citations were read aloud on slides and were not checked against the papers in this ingest. Correlation across a speed range partly reflects the fact that running faster *requires* a faster limb swing — it is close to a description of speed rather than a separate cause of it. Do not coach "paw back" as a cue in isolation: the live session records the common failure where athletes cast the foot out in front and pull it back, which lands the foot ahead of the hips. Moyer says he teaches pawback only when needed, and always with the foot landing as close under the body as possible.
**Example** — Two receivers top out at 9.1 m/s on GPS. On side film one shows a high thigh and fast retraction; the other's thigh barely passes horizontal and the foot drops straight down. The second athlete is the candidate for knee-drive and retraction work, and his next GPS top speed is the check.
**Related** — [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]] — the same thigh action is what Moyer says fails first under fatigue.
=== claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver
# The Ankle Plantar Flexors as the Main "Driving Link" at Top Speed
**What it is** — Moyer's case that the foot and ankle, not the knee, drive the push-off at maximal speed. He strings together figures from several sources:
- Soleus and gastrocnemius generate **77% of vertical and 60% of horizontal** centre-of-mass acceleration; the soleus gives vertical support at all speeds, the gastrocnemius more horizontal propulsion.
- The Achilles tendon "accumulates **75–90%** of the mechanical energy" (source not named).
- From a 1981 *Soviet Sports Review* article out of Zatsiorsky's lab: during takeoff external energy rises by **340 J**; knee muscles do **31 J**, plantar flexors **192 J** ("more than six times as much"), so "the main driving link in running with maximum sustained speed is the foot". The foot-ankle returns **60–70%** of the landing energy.
- Push-off "can generate up to **20%** of the force" in sprinting (attributed to Yessis; Moyer says in the live session he does not know where that figure came from).
**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: the foot and ankle work eccentrically then concentrically in each contact, storing energy in the tendon as the body passes over the foot and giving it back at push-off. The training conclusion he draws is to develop the "spring-like properties of the foot, calves and tendons" — calf strength, ankle plyometrics, foot work.
**When to apply** — As a reason to keep calf, Achilles and foot work in a speed programme (single-leg calf raises, ankle-dominant plyometrics, isometrics), and to look at the ankle when an athlete sinks at contact.
**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: these are force- and energy-share figures quoted from slides, mixing different measures (muscle contribution to acceleration, tendon energy storage, joint work) from different studies and different speeds, none checked in this ingest. They cannot be added together, and "20% of the force" sits awkwardly next to "192 of 340 J". The 77%/60% figure resembles musculoskeletal-modelling results (e.g. Dorn, Schache and Pandy's running simulations), which are model outputs, not measurements. Joint-work studies of maximal sprinting generally find the **hip** dominates at the highest speeds, with the ankle's share plateauing — so "the foot is the main driver" should not be repeated as settled. The practical advice (train the calf-Achilles complex) does not depend on these numbers being right.
**Example** — A running back's contact looks soft on film and his ankle collapses. Moyer's framework says train the calf-Achilles spring; a sound version of that is to add single-leg calf strength and ankle hops and re-film, without citing "the Achilles does 90% of the work" to the athlete.
**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — ankle extension is the third local key action. The knee-extension-at-toe-off argument that Moyer builds on these figures (knee should not exceed ~165°) is covered in a separate, contested entry.
=== framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles
# Four Acceleration Profiles (After J. J. Wild) as a Starting Point for Training
**What it is** — Moyer uses J. J. Wild's research (introduced to him by Jonas Dodoo's Speedworks group) that sorts team-sport athletes' early-acceleration strategies into four groups from step length, step rate, contact time and flight time. His labels and descriptions:
1. **Bounders — step length + air-based.** Long strides and good projection, but they pop up vertically; hips rise too early.
2. **Drivers — step length + ground-based.** Long strides and good projection, but very little air time; hips stay low with no rise; "mushy", not bouncy.
3. **Spinners — step frequency + ground-based.** Quick steps that "spin the wheels"; the foot barely leaves the ground.
4. **Bouncers — step frequency + air-based.** Quick steps but bouncing up and down; looks like jumping. He also calls this the "Fred Flintstone" runner (he uses that label loosely elsewhere).
His training response is to **move each athlete toward the middle**, not into a best quadrant: bounders a little more ground-based (more force into the ground, especially in acceleration); drivers a little more bouncy; spinners better projection plus a bit more bounce; bouncers better projection and more force. **Why it works** — Categorising reduces complexity (he quotes Stu McMillan): in a squad of 20–40, four buckets let you individualise the first 10–15 minutes of a session with four or five group-specific exercises while the rest of the plan stays common.

His training response per bucket is his own opinion; responses for spinners and bouncers were stated only in outline. Do not use the bucket to predict injury (see [[claim--acceleration-profile-predicts-injury-site]]).
**Example** — Of 16 skill players, four are bounders. In the first 12 minutes of speed day they do heavy sled marches and single-leg calf raises while the drivers do pogo series and pawback drills; everyone then runs the common acceleration session.
**Related** — [[principle--individualization]] (periodization--bompa) — agreement: individualise where capacities genuinely diverge; buckets are a cheap middle ground.

=== framework--isolate-integrate-improvise-sprint-technique
# Isolate → Integrate → Improvise: Moving a New Sprint Pattern Into the Game
**What it is** — Moyer's three-stage progression for a changed technique (from Ido Portal's "3 I" framing; Moyer calls it "breaking bad"). Worked example: heel strike → midfoot/forefoot.
1. **Isolate.** Straight line, full conscious attention, old-way/new-way contrast ([[heuristic--old-way-new-way-heel-strike-sprint]]). **Ramp speed by self-rated effort**: the athlete's first jog is usually "30–40%", then 50% → 75% → 90% → 100%. Move up only if the new pattern holds with "technical proficiency." Slow to fast, short to long. "Learning isn't done at 100% speed", because "you lose sensory information" at max speed, and mechanics change with velocity.
2. **Integrate.** Only after **repeated 100% sprints across multiple sessions** hold the pattern, add complexity **slowly**, one stimulus at a time: arms overhead → shoulders and head turned while the legs run straight → arms across chest → holding a stick or ball → being chased in a straight line → chasing someone in a straight line.
3. **Improvise.** Zig-zag chases, changing directions while chasing or being chased, catching or kicking a ball. Then small-sided → medium → large-sided games that "resemble a practice." Here he switches to a "nonlinear... differential learning, constraints-led, ecological approach" and perception–action coupling.
**The regression rule:** if a new stimulus brings back the old pattern (e.g., chasing a teammate, "now they're not thinking about heel striking"), **scale back complexity**. The pattern has not yet moved from conscious competence to unconscious competence.
**Why it works** — As asserted: Early on, the new pattern needs attention. Any competing demand (speed, a ball, an opponent) takes attention away, and the old pattern, which is stronger, wins (proactive interference). Adding demands one at a time lets the new pattern become robust to each before the next. The staging and the "conscious → unconscious competence" idea are practitioner models. Moyer shows before/after film but no controlled comparison.
**When to apply** — Sprint-technique changes in any football player. It maps cleanly onto late-stage RTP: straight-line %-effort ramps (already standard in return-to-run) → sport-specific constraints (ball, turned head, pursuit angles) → reactive, opposed drills → team periods. The regression rule gives a clear decision point: if the old pattern returns in a reactive drill, go back a step rather than pushing through.
**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The Myszka authors argue that isolating a skill from its information (the straight-line, unopposed isolate stage) teaches attunement to the wrong information, and that task *simplification* (keep a chaser, change the distance) beats *decomposition*. On their evidence, the isolate stage should be brief or should keep a chaser from the start. Moyer's counter is that his isolate stage targets a *mechanical* fault in a closed, cyclic action, where "the information" is largely internal. And the CLA studies test game skills, not unlearning an entrenched pattern. Neither side has direct evidence for sprint-pattern change. Practical limits: the self-rated %-effort scale is unreliable (athletes misjudge 75% vs. 90%). Requiring "multiple sessions at 100%" before any integration can use up a whole off-season. And his integrate list is arbitrary in order. Choose stimuli that match the athlete's position.
**Example** — A DB fixing a heel strike. Weeks 1–2: 50/75/90/100% build-ups with old/new contrast. Week 3: backpedal-turn-and-run with head over the shoulder, then pursuit of a ball-carrier on a fixed angle. Week 4: 1v1 open-field tag in a 10×10 yd box. When he chases a receiver and lands on his heel, go back to fixed-angle pursuit for a week.
**Related** — [[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]] and [[claim--fundamentals-do-not-require-decomposition]] — tension over the isolate stage; [[heuristic--contextual-sprint-work]] — agreement: chasers are the key integration stimulus; [[principle--movement-ownership-speed]] — agreement that learning happens below maximum speed.
=== heuristic--check-retention-not-cue-delivery-sprint
# Judge a Sprint Intervention by Whether the Action Changed and Stayed Changed
**What it is** — A thread across Lesson 10 and the live sessions. Three checks follow from it:
1. **The action changed, not the cue delivered.** Giving a cue is not coaching. The test is whether the next rep *looks* different on film. Moyer's standard for any coach: "show me the before, tell me what the intervention was, and let's see what we got."
2. **Immediate change ≠ learning.** On an arm-action cue in Live 2: "What is the long-term retention of that learning from that one cue?... Learning's done through retention. If they can replicate it in the next run, awesome. But what about next week?" In Live 3, he adds that an athlete can show a cued change in the drill, then revert "as soon as you give them that same drill or a cognitive task."
3. **Fade the support and see if the action holds.** His wicket fade: after a run of **10–15 wickets**, remove the **last five** and tell the athlete to keep running "as if they were still there". Then remove the next five. Hurdles have to go eventually, "they're not sprinting a hurdle."
**Why it works** — Performance during practice reflects temporary support: the cue in working memory, the wicket forcing the fold. Learning is what remains when the support is gone and time has passed. This performance/learning distinction is well established in motor-learning research. Moyer's fade gives a within-session transfer test: the wicket-free section shows whether the athlete can produce the action from the feel alone.
**When to apply** — Evaluating any technical intervention, including your own: re-film the *next session*, not just the next rep. In RTP, a mechanic that appears only straight after a cue should not count as restored. Wicket and band progressions should always have a planned fade.
**When NOT to apply** — Moyer undercuts this himself by treating "that feels better" as "gold". An athlete's report is an *immediate* signal and often does not match the film. Use it to pick the next rep, not to judge learning. A retention check a week later is also confounded by fatigue and by whatever else changed that week. Compare like with like (same distance, timing, fatigue state). Finally, this is not an argument against cues: a cue that only works acutely can still be useful as a pre-rep reminder.
**Example** — Tuesday: a receiver runs 12 wickets with good fold, then 3 reps with the last 4 removed. Film shows the fold holds for two steps past the last wicket. Thursday: fly-20 with no wickets, filmed from the side. The fold is there on two of three reps, so the change is partly retained. Keep the wicket block for another week before fading further.
**Related** — [[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] — agreement that practising one fixed movement is not the target; [[framework--three-training-effects]] — the immediate/delayed/cumulative split, applied here to skill rather than fitness.
=== framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality
# The Sprint Correctives Menu, Organised by Quality
**What it is** — Moyer's troubleshooting sheet (a PDF in the course, walked through in Lesson 9 and again in Live 3 ~1–60 min). For each global quality, the menu gives: the faults that flag it, what range to check first, then technical drills, cues, strength exercises and where to place wearable load. It is his menu, drawn from Yessis, Verkhoshansky, Natera and his own practice. He invites coaches to add their own.
| Quality | Faults that flag it | Check first | Technical drills | Cues | Strength | Wearable placement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Projection** | Short stride; little centre-of-mass travel | Hip extension (Thomas), hip flexion, dorsiflexion bent- and straight-knee, plantar flexion, big toe, all passive vs. active | Broad jumps (single/repeat); **heavy sled sprints** (load-velocity profiled), short accels; resisted bounding; wall acceleration drills → banded; heavy sled pushes (only if no room to sprint); leaps/bounds for distance | Push the ground away; push through the ground; stay on the ground as long as possible; explode; sprint up a hill; (Live 3) lead with your belt buckle, drive hips forward | Wall accels; hip extension (bridges); calf raises seated and standing, single and double leg (ankles are "more times than not" the limit); Yessis lunges (back leg straight, lead with hips), isometric holds if hip-extension range is short; banded front lunges (Active Cords); barbell front lunges; explosive front lunges | **Front of thigh + front of calf** |
| **Reactivity / stiffness** | Heel strike; poor trunk discipline (leaning, rounded); soft collapsing stance (ankle "mush"); knee locked at toe-off | Range "isn't usually going to be a problem"; this is a strength quality | Build-up sprints for frequency; overhead PVC/med-ball/arms-up sprints and wickets; single-leg jumps; extensive jumps; depth jumps (Verkhoshansky); pogos | Be quick off the ground; bounce; snap the ground like a whip | Yessis delay squats; K-Box (flywheel) squats; Natera ISO foot holds and mid-thigh pulls | **Vest (heavy, vertical load) + weights all around the ankle/calf** |
| **Switching: knee drive** | Low thigh height; long lever | Hip flexion; hamstring at the knee, passive vs. active | Dribbling drills; banded bounding; wicket runs (with wearable load); switch jumps (Live 3: band-resisted in a squat rack rather than over boxes) | Break the glass; throw a knee; sprint up a hill; drive the thigh hard | Yessis knee drives; Russian special strength; reverse crunches (lower abs, posterior tilt; build to 50 reps → ankle weights → band); explosive front lunge + knee drive; hamstring PAILs/RAILs for a long lever | **Front of thigh; posterior calf** (to force the fold) |
| **Switching: pawback** | Foot drops instead of attacking; lands far in front of hips; "straight down, not back and down" | Hip flexion; hamstrings | Scissor runs; banded bounding; banded marches; speed bounding; wicket runs; switch jumps | Snap the ground like a whip; hammer the nail; hit the ground hard | Yessis pawbacks; Natera ISO hamstrings; GHRs (setup: hamstring origin hanging *in front of* the pad for a double contraction); banded retractions (acceleration); bridges incl. single-leg; hip-flexion PAILs/RAILs | **Posterior shorts (hamstrings/glutes) + posterior calf** |
| **Toe-off (ankle extension)** | Knee extends at toe-off; foot turns out, pushing off the side of the foot | Dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, big toe; **tibial rotation** | "Bart walks" (banded low-lunge walks driving through the big toe; Chris Korfist's name for them is uncertain in the transcript); 45° banded walks/bounds | Push the ground away | Single-leg calf raises with the foot straight and pressure through the big toe; Natera foot isos (done "every day") | **Around the ankles**; for a turned-out foot, wrap calf loads **obliquely**, heavy end toward the medial malleolus |
Standing rules that go with the table: **sled sprints over sled pushes** when there is a choice (the only reason given for pushes is weather and space). **"Load the problem"** with wearable resistance. **If the foot turns out, check the tibia before any drills**, because "none of those technical drills... is going to work if the issue stems from the knee down."
**Why it works** — The menu puts one idea into operation. A global fault has several possible causes (range, strength, coordination, awareness), so it offers one or more options per cause and orders them range → drills/strength → cues/load. The pairing of each quality with its muscles and joint actions is taken from the course's biomechanics. That each exercise fixes its fault is Moyer's practice claim, supported by his before/after films, not by controlled comparison.
**When to apply** — Writing individual "first 10–15 minutes" add-ons inside a team lift. In Live 3 Moyer shows bucketing a 16-player group into four profile groups with 4–5 exercises each; see [[framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles]]. RTP late stages: pick the row that matches the athlete's pre-injury film fault. Staff education: it is a ready common language between Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine.
**When NOT to apply** — This is a menu, not a diagnosis. Several rows share exercises (wickets, banded bounding, switch jumps), so a "fix" cannot confirm which cause was real. Several items rest on contested claims: the knee should stay bent at toe-off (disputed within the course); "posturology", i.e. an out-turned foot that PAILs/RAILs and soft-tissue work do not fix is "a postural issue" linked to "the feet and the eyes", which is his opinion with no evidence offered; and wearable placements are rules of thumb from a product he promotes. Heavy vest loading and depth jumps for stiffness need the landing and tissue tolerance a returning athlete may not yet have.
**Example** — A tight end lands with his foot far in front of his hips and drops it rather than attacking. Switching/pawback row: check hip-flexion and hamstring range (both fine). Then 2×/week banded pawbacks and GHRs, wicket runs with posterior-calf loading, and the cue "hammer the nail". Re-film in three weeks.
**Related** — [[heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint]] — decides whether the "check first" column or the drills columns apply; [[framework--isometric-set-positions-ankle-knee-hip]] — the Natera isometrics the menu links to.
=== heuristic--accentuation-band-setup-knee-drive-pawback-sprint
# Accentuation: Load the Knee Drive and Pawback Where the Sprint Needs Force
**What it is** — The principle of accentuation (Zatsiorsky, *Science and Practice of Strength Training*), which Moyer uses as the design rule for special strength exercises: **train strength through the part of the range where the sport movement needs maximal force**, not through the full anatomical range. In running, muscles are active over a narrow range, and peak activity is near the end-points of angular motion. Zatsiorsky's own example is the swing leg: hip flexion is accentuated *before* the thigh reaches vertical and decelerated after it. So there is no reason to build hip-flexor strength beyond that range, or at the weakest position (as the "peak contraction principle" would suggest), because in that range the *extensors*, not the flexors, are working. The two band exercises that follow from it, and their setup rules:
- **Knee drive** — band anchored at **knee height**. The athlete starts with the thigh *behind* the body, folds the leg, and drives the thigh forward.
- **Pawback** — band anchored **high enough that the foot travels back *and down***, not just back, because that is the path of the foot into the ground when sprinting. Cue: "whip from the hip." For acceleration the variation starts thigh-up and attacks down. For upright running it is cycled quickly from a leg-out-front start.
- Verkhoshansky's 1986 demonstration (shown in Lesson 8) combines both actions in one exercise. In Live 3, Moyer shows a weighted-foot-strap ("Monkey Feet") version of it.
**Why it works** — Strength is joint-angle specific. Loading a movement where the sprint loads it gives more shared elements (see [[principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill]]) and less wasted work. The band's line of pull decides which part of the range is loaded, so the anchor height is not a detail. It *is* the exercise. The angle-specificity mechanism is textbook. That these particular band setups transfer to sprint mechanics is Moyer's practice claim.

=== framework--isolate-integrate-improvise-sprint-technique
# Isolate → Integrate → Improvise: Moving a New Sprint Pattern Into the Game
**What it is** — Moyer's three-stage progression for a changed technique (from Ido Portal's "3 I" framing; Moyer calls it "breaking bad"). Worked example: heel strike → midfoot/forefoot.
1. **Isolate.** Straight line, full conscious attention, old-way/new-way contrast ([[heuristic--old-way-new-way-heel-strike-sprint]]). **Ramp speed by self-rated effort**: the athlete's first jog is usually "30–40%", then 50% → 75% → 90% → 100%. Move up only if the new pattern holds with "technical proficiency." Slow to fast, short to long. "Learning isn't done at 100% speed", because "you lose sensory information" at max speed, and mechanics change with velocity.
2. **Integrate.** Only after **repeated 100% sprints across multiple sessions** hold the pattern, add complexity **slowly**, one stimulus at a time: arms overhead → shoulders and head turned while the legs run straight → arms across chest → holding a stick or ball → being chased in a straight line → chasing someone in a straight line.
3. **Improvise.** Zig-zag chases, changing directions while chasing or being chased, catching or kicking a ball. Then small-sided → medium → large-sided games that "resemble a practice." Here he switches to a "nonlinear... differential learning, constraints-led, ecological approach" and perception–action coupling.
**The regression rule:** if a new stimulus brings back the old pattern (e.g., chasing a teammate, "now they're not thinking about heel striking"), **scale back complexity**. The pattern has not yet moved from conscious competence to unconscious competence.
**Why it works** — As asserted: Early on, the new pattern needs attention. Any competing demand (speed, a ball, an opponent) takes attention away, and the old pattern, which is stronger, wins (proactive interference). Adding demands one at a time lets the new pattern become robust to each before the next. The staging and the "conscious → unconscious competence" idea are practitioner models. Moyer shows before/after film but no controlled comparison.
**When to apply** — Sprint-technique changes in any football player. It maps cleanly onto late-stage RTP: straight-line %-effort ramps (already standard in return-to-run) → sport-specific constraints (ball, turned head, pursuit angles) → reactive, opposed drills → team periods. The regression rule gives a clear decision point: if the old pattern returns in a reactive drill, go back a step rather than pushing through.
**When NOT to apply** — **Contested.** The Myszka authors argue that isolating a skill from its information (the straight-line, unopposed isolate stage) teaches attunement to the wrong information, and that task *simplification* (keep a chaser, change the distance) beats *decomposition*. On their evidence, the isolate stage should be brief or should keep a chaser from the start. Moyer's counter is that his isolate stage targets a *mechanical* fault in a closed, cyclic action, where "the information" is largely internal. And the CLA studies test game skills, not unlearning an entrenched pattern. Neither side has direct evidence for sprint-pattern change. Practical limits: the self-rated %-effort scale is unreliable (athletes misjudge 75% vs. 90%). Requiring "multiple sessions at 100%" before any integration can use up a whole off-season. And his integrate list is arbitrary in order. Choose stimuli that match the athlete's position.
**Example** — A DB fixing a heel strike. Weeks 1–2: 50/75/90/100% build-ups with old/new contrast. Week 3: backpedal-turn-and-run with head over the shoulder, then pursuit of a ball-carrier on a fixed angle. Week 4: 1v1 open-field tag in a 10×10 yd box. When he chases a receiver and lands on his heel, go back to fixed-angle pursuit for a week.
**Related** — [[principle--task-simplification-not-decomposition]] and [[claim--fundamentals-do-not-require-decomposition]] — tension over the isolate stage; [[heuristic--contextual-sprint-work]] — agreement: chasers are the key integration stimulus; [[principle--movement-ownership-speed]] — agreement that learning happens below maximum speed.
=== heuristic--check-retention-not-cue-delivery-sprint
# Judge a Sprint Intervention by Whether the Action Changed and Stayed Changed
**What it is** — A thread across Lesson 10 and the live sessions. Three checks follow from it:
1. **The action changed, not the cue delivered.** Giving a cue is not coaching. The test is whether the next rep *looks* different on film. Moyer's standard for any coach: "show me the before, tell me what the intervention was, and let's see what we got."
2. **Immediate change ≠ learning.** On an arm-action cue in Live 2: "What is the long-term retention of that learning from that one cue?... Learning's done through retention. If they can replicate it in the next run, awesome. But what about next week?" In Live 3, he adds that an athlete can show a cued change in the drill, then revert "as soon as you give them that same drill or a cognitive task."
3. **Fade the support and see if the action holds.** His wicket fade: after a run of **10–15 wickets**, remove the **last five** and tell the athlete to keep running "as if they were still there". Then remove the next five. Hurdles have to go eventually, "they're not sprinting a hurdle."
**Why it works** — Performance during practice reflects temporary support: the cue in working memory, the wicket forcing the fold. Learning is what remains when the support is gone and time has passed. This performance/learning distinction is well established in motor-learning research. Moyer's fade gives a within-session transfer test: the wicket-free section shows whether the athlete can produce the action from the feel alone.
**When to apply** — Evaluating any technical intervention, including your own: re-film the *next session*, not just the next rep. In RTP, a mechanic that appears only straight after a cue should not count as restored. Wicket and band progressions should always have a planned fade.
**When NOT to apply** — Moyer undercuts this himself by treating "that feels better" as "gold". An athlete's report is an *immediate* signal and often does not match the film. Use it to pick the next rep, not to judge learning. A retention check a week later is also confounded by fatigue and by whatever else changed that week. Compare like with like (same distance, timing, fatigue state). Finally, this is not an argument against cues: a cue that only works acutely can still be useful as a pre-rep reminder.
**Example** — Tuesday: a receiver runs 12 wickets with good fold, then 3 reps with the last 4 removed. Film shows the fold holds for two steps past the last wicket. Thursday: fly-20 with no wickets, filmed from the side. The fold is there on two of three reps, so the change is partly retained. Keep the wicket block for another week before fading further.
**Related** — [[principle--repetition-without-repetition]] — agreement that practising one fixed movement is not the target; [[framework--three-training-effects]] — the immediate/delayed/cumulative split, applied here to skill rather than fitness.
=== framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality
# The Sprint Correctives Menu, Organised by Quality
**What it is** — Moyer's troubleshooting sheet (a PDF in the course, walked through in Lesson 9 and again in Live 3 ~1–60 min). For each global quality, the menu gives: the faults that flag it, what range to check first, then technical drills, cues, strength exercises and where to place wearable load. It is his menu, drawn from Yessis, Verkhoshansky, Natera and his own practice. He invites coaches to add their own.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Projection** | Short stride; little centre-of-mass travel | Hip extension (Thomas), hip flexion, dorsiflexion bent- and straight-knee, plantar flexion, big toe, all passive vs. active | Broad jumps (single/repeat); **heavy sled sprints** (load-velocity profiled), short accels; resisted bounding; wall acceleration drills → banded; heavy sled pushes (only if no room to sprint); leaps/bounds for distance | Push the ground away; push through the ground; stay on the ground as long as possible; explode; sprint up a hill; (Live 3) lead with your belt buckle, drive hips forward | Wall accels; hip extension (bridges); calf raises seated and standing, single and double leg (ankles are "more times than not" the limit); Yessis lunges (back leg straight, lead with hips), isometric holds if hip-extension range is short; banded front lunges (Active Cords); barbell front lunges; explosive front lunges | **Front of thigh + front of calf** |
| **Reactivity / stiffness** | Heel strike; poor trunk discipline (leaning, rounded); soft collapsing stance (ankle "mush"); knee locked at toe-off | Range "isn't usually going to be a problem"; this is a strength quality | Build-up sprints for frequency; overhead PVC/med-ball/arms-up sprints and wickets; single-leg jumps; extensive jumps; depth jumps (Verkhoshansky); pogos | Be quick off the ground; bounce; snap the ground like a whip | Yessis delay squats; K-Box (flywheel) squats; Natera ISO foot holds and mid-thigh pulls | **Vest (heavy, vertical load) + weights all around the ankle/calf** |
| **Switching: knee drive** | Low thigh height; long lever | Hip flexion; hamstring at the knee, passive vs. active | Dribbling drills; banded bounding; wicket runs (with wearable load); switch jumps (Live 3: band-resisted in a squat rack rather than over boxes) | Break the glass; throw a knee; sprint up a hill; drive the thigh hard | Yessis knee drives; Russian special strength; reverse crunches (lower abs, posterior tilt; build to 50 reps → ankle weights → band); explosive front lunge + knee drive; hamstring PAILs/RAILs for a long lever | **Front of thigh; posterior calf** (to force the fold) |
| **Switching: pawback** | Foot drops instead of attacking; lands far in front of hips; "straight down, not back and down" | Hip flexion; hamstrings | Scissor runs; banded bounding; banded marches; speed bounding; wicket runs; switch jumps | Snap the ground like a whip; hammer the nail; hit the ground hard | Yessis pawbacks; Natera ISO hamstrings; GHRs (setup: hamstring origin hanging *in front of* the pad for a double contraction); banded retractions (acceleration); bridges incl. single-leg; hip-flexion PAILs/RAILs | **Posterior shorts (hamstrings/glutes) + posterior calf** |

The pairing of each quality with its muscles and joint actions is taken from the course's biomechanics. That each exercise fixes its fault is Moyer's practice claim, supported by his before/after films, not by controlled comparison.
**When to apply** — Writing individual "first 10–15 minutes" add-ons inside a team lift. In Live 3 Moyer shows bucketing a 16-player group into four profile groups with 4–5 exercises each; see [[framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles]]. === heuristic--accentuation-band-setup-knee-drive-pawback-sprint
# Accentuation: Load the Knee Drive and Pawback Where the Sprint Needs Force
**What it is** — The principle of accentuation (Zatsiorsky, *Science and Practice of Strength Training*), which Moyer uses as the design rule for special strength exercises: **train strength through the part of the range where the sport movement needs maximal force**, not through the full anatomical range. So there is no reason to build hip-flexor strength beyond that range, or at the weakest position (as the "peak contraction principle" would suggest), because in that range the *extensors*, not the flexors, are working. === principle--sprint-muscles-work-as-dimmers-not-switches
**What it is** — Yessis's teaching point, passed on by Moyer: during the sprint cycle muscles do not snap on and off. They **dim up** as a joint action approaches, peak, and **dim down** as the limb passes the point where the opposing group must take over. The hamstrings, for example, build tension in mid-to-late swing to stop the thigh and pull the leg down and back, stay active through early stance, then fade once the thigh is behind the pelvis so the hip flexors can load and drive it forward. Moyer shows a Soviet EMG timing chart beside a 2017 review of sprint EMG studies and says the two patterns look very similar.
**Why it works** — Graded, overlapping activation is well supported by the sprint EMG literature. Moyer's mechanism — "we can't have muscles on opposite sides of a joint both maximally contracted; something has to calm down" — is **asserted, not shown**, and is too absolute: co-contraction around the knee and ankle in stance is real and useful for joint stiffness. The better reading is that **peaks** of opposing groups are staggered, not that one group falls silent.
**When NOT to apply** — The dimmer picture tells you *when* a muscle is active, not *how hard*, *how it is changing length*, or what training will transfer (see the EMG entry). Surface EMG timing also varies with speed, fatigue and electrode placement; do not over-read one chart. And it is descriptive: it will not tell you why a given athlete's pattern is faulty.
=== principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill
**What it is** — Moyer frames every exercise-selection argument as a transfer-of-training question and splits transfer into two kinds that get argued as if they were one. **Physical-ability transfer** asks whether getting stronger or more powerful carries over to sprinting ("does squatting make you faster?"). **Motor-skill transfer** asks whether an exercise changes *how* the athlete sprints: thigh height, pawback, foot contact. Both are graded the usual way: **positive** (training helps the target), **negative** (training hinders it), **zero** (no effect), and **near vs. far** (how similar the training context is to the target). Three things drive transfer: movement similarity, sensory similarity and cognitive factors. His central claim, taken from Bondarchuk, is that **motor-skill transfer is more specific than physical-ability transfer.** An exercise can build useful capacity and still leave technique untouched. Exercises are judged by the outcome they produce in the sprint, not by how hard or impressive they look.
**Why it works** — The mechanism he offers is the theory of identical elements (Thorndike & Woodworth, 1901): transfer scales with the number of elements two tasks share. Force capacity is a shared element for many tasks. A coordination pattern is shared only with tasks that have the same joint actions, timing and sensory feedback, so skill transfer drops off faster with distance. This is asserted from the Soviet transfer literature and educational psychology. The course does not show the data.
**When NOT to apply** — "Negative transfer" is easy to invoke and hard to show. Moyer offers no measured case of a strength exercise making sprint technique worse, only Bondarchuk's questionnaire finding and his own film judgement. Do not use the label to ban a lift from a football program without evidence that sprint outcomes actually fell. Near/far here is about *movement* similarity. The Myszka entries argue that the *perceptual* similarity to the game matters more for football, and a straight-line sprint drill is itself far from game running.
=== heuristic--sprint-video-setup-stationary-camera
**What it is** — Moyer's capture advice, given to participants in Live 1 after some of their clips came back blurry:
**Why it works** — A fixed camera keeps the background stationary, so posture and limb angles are not distorted by panning, and the same setup can be repeated for a before/after comparison. Distance reduces perspective distortion and keeps the whole stride in frame. Front and back views catch frontal-plane faults (crossover, hip drop, foot placement) a side view hides. This is standard 2D video practice; Moyer gives **no frame rate, lens, height or distance specification** beyond these rules of thumb.
**When NOT to apply** — A fixed camera trades field of view for accuracy; for full 40-yard or game-speed runs you will need several fixed cameras or a pan and must accept distortion. Phone video at low frame rates will not resolve ground contact reliably at top speed; the advice is about setup, not measurement. For football-specific movement (breaking on a ball, pursuit), game or practice film from multiple angles matters more than a clean track clip.
=== claim--narrow-quarter-squat-transfers-to-sprint
**What it is** — Moyer's worked example of "it depends" in the strength-vs-speed debate: "studies have shown that quarter squatting with a narrow stance transfers better to speed and jumping than does wide squatting." He does not drop full or wide squatting. Lower-level athletes still get general transfer from it. But **as competition approaches, his squatting becomes narrower and shallower**, moving toward a quarter squat. The same partial-range logic runs through his special-strength choices: Yessis delay squats go only to about quarter depth.
**Why it works** — Two mechanisms are implied. Neither is demonstrated in the course. (1) Identical elements: a narrow, shallow squat is closer to sprint stance-leg joint angles and foot position. (2) Accentuation ([[heuristic--accentuation-band-setup-knee-drive-pawback-sprint]]): train strength where the sport needs peak force, not across a full range the sprint never uses.
**When NOT to apply** — Moyer names no study. There is a partial-vs-full squat literature, but its transfer results are mixed and it was not checked for this entry. Treat "transfers better" as unverified. Partial squats let athletes handle very large loads, which brings spinal-load and technique-drift risk for heavy linemen. Full-range work still has hypertrophy and joint-range value that a quarter squat does not replace, especially after injury, when restoring full knee and hip range is a rehab goal in its own right. The stance-width claim may not apply to positions whose sport stance is wide (OL, DL).
47:**Example** — Summer testing: each player's flying 10 is filmed side-on at 240 fps plus one front view. A graduate assistant ticks the checklist per athlete; athletes with three or more flags go to a follow-up range-of-motion check ([[heuristic--match-sprint-fault-to-rom-check-before-intervening]]).

# Fundamentals of Sprinting (Moyer, Strength Coach Network) — ingest map

A paid video course, not a book. "Chapter" = lesson number. Source text is the
checked machine transcript for each lesson (independent ASR compared against the
player captions, ~91–95% word agreement). Nobody listened back to the audio.
Lesson 16 had no caption track, so its transcript is single-source.

**Confidence rule for this whole source (set 2026-09-25, applies to every entry):**
- This is a practitioner lecture course. Its mechanisms, percentages and injury links
  are the instructor's claims, not results that were checked against the cited studies.
- **Ceiling is `supported`** even though the tier is full-text. Nothing from this course is `proven`.
- **`untested`** for causal claims: heel strike or long swing-leg lever → hamstring injury;
  wearable resistance → faster sprinting; force- and energy-share percentages; the
  loaded-squat vs. wearable-load kinetic-energy comparison (dimensionally inconsistent as spoken);
  before/after cases with several concurrent changes.
- **`contested`** where the transcripts record a live dispute: knee extension at toe-off;
  whether the hamstring works isometrically in late swing.
- Product mentions (wearable resistance, timing gates, analysis software) are commercial
  context, not evidence. Moyer sells wearable-resistance coaching — note the conflict where relevant.

A paid video course, not a book. "Chapter" = lesson number. Source text is the
checked machine transcript for each lesson (independent ASR compared against the
player captions, ~91–95% word agreement). Nobody listened back to the audio.
Lesson 16 had no caption track, so its transcript is single-source.

**Confidence rule for this whole source (set 2026-09-25, applies to every entry):**
- This is a practitioner lecture course. Its mechanisms, percentages and injury links
  are the instructor's claims, not results that were checked against the cited studies.
- **Ceiling is `supported`** even though the tier is full-text. Nothing from this course is `proven`.
- **`untested`** for causal claims: heel strike or long swing-leg lever → hamstring injury;
  wearable resistance → faster sprinting; force- and energy-share percentages; the
  loaded-squat vs. wearable-load kinetic-energy comparison (dimensionally inconsistent as spoken);
  before/after cases with several concurrent changes.
- **`contested`** where the transcripts record a live dispute: knee extension at toe-off;
  whether the hamstring works isometrically in late swing.
- Product mentions (wearable resistance, timing gates, analysis software) are commercial
  context, not evidence. Moyer sells wearable-resistance coaching — note the conflict where relevant.

**[09:19]** Here's an example. As I mentioned before, with the knee drive, and one of the things that I have found anecdotally that I have not seen any research done is swinging along lever with hamstring injuries. Now, chicken to the egg. This is a young girl that had a left hamstring issues, and so I wanted to look at how she ran, and she had swinging a long lever, right? As you can see the difference, that her left leg does not fold up nearly as well as her right leg, and it just kind of crashes forward. And with the NFL football player that I did the video analysis of before, he had the same thing. He had a history of hamstring issues with the one leg, and you can see that he was swinging along lever. Now, was he swinging along lever because he had the hamstring issues

**[10:04]** or did the long lever cause the hamstring issues? I don't know, but I have seen enough in my 15 years of looking at doing technique analysis that there is a correlation between the two. And here's an example of that football player who had the history of hamstring issues, right? And you can see left leg doesn't fold up nearly as well, swinging a long lever, having to open early and attack the ground a little early compared to the right leg. Now, here's some interesting research done by the Soviets in a 1989 Soviet sports review, looking at, okay, now what are the fatigue-inducing changes in sprinting technique? So how does technique change as the athlete fatigues? And what are the key mechanisms at that?

=== framework--sprint-joint-actions-by-phase
**What it is** — Moyer's (and Yessis's) upright-sprint map of what the pelvis, hip, knee and ankle do in each phase, and which muscles are dimming up or down. Summarised from Lesson 4, cross-checked against its rework in Live 2:
| Phase | Pelvis | Hip | Knee | Ankle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Toe-off** | Anterior tilt (erectors) | Extension; glutes/hamstrings **dimming down**, hip flexors building tension to stop the thigh going further back | Slight flexion; quads roughly isometric | Plantar flexion (gastrocnemius, soleus) |
| **Early swing** | Posterior tilt begins (abdominals) | Flexion (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) | Flexion, largely passive, so the leg folds into a **short lever** | — |
| **Mid swing** | Posterior tilt (abdominals assist) | Flexion carried mainly by **momentum** of the initial contraction; hamstrings start building tension to stop the thigh | Extension as the shin swings out | — |
| **Late swing** | Anterior tilt (erectors) | Extension, down and back; **glute max and hamstrings most active** | Shin reaching toward contact | Plantar flexion |
| **Stance** | Anterior tilt | Extension; glutes/hamstrings working eccentric to quasi-isometric | Flexion; quads quasi-isometric to resist collapse | Plantar flexion; tibialis, gastrocnemius, soleus act as brakes |
**Why it works** — Knowing the joint action, its range and which muscles are loading lets you pick exercises that match a phase and diagnose whether a fault is technical or a strength deficit. The structure is standard gait-cycle kinesiology; the muscle roles are broadly consistent with sprint EMG data. Details below are where Moyer's version is loose.
**When NOT to apply** — **Do not quote this table as anatomy of record.** The lesson contains errors that are Moyer's, not the transcript's (they recur in Live 2): at stance he credits **glutes and hamstrings** with *anterior* pelvic tilt, although his own opening definition lists them as *posterior* tilters; he places plantar/dorsiflexion at the subtalar joint (it is the talocrural joint); and his late-swing knee is described as "flexion, quads isometric," which reads like stance, not swing. The lesson header also notes anatomical terms were standardised from context. It is an **upright-sprint** map; acceleration and football-specific starts differ. And it is qualitative: no joint angles or velocities are given beyond the contested knee figure.
=== framework--soviet-lineage-of-sprint-training-ideas
**What it is** — Moyer's map of whose ideas sit under current speed and strength practice. Use it to **trace a modern concept back to its source** before judging it.
| Figure | What Moyer credits them with | Where it shows up now |
|---|---|---|
| **Lev Matveyev** | *Fundamentals of Sports Training* (Russian 1965, English c. 1981); **general vs. specific training** | Linear periodization; the general/special exercise split |
| **Vladimir Zatsiorsky** | Soviet school of biomechanics; *Science and Practice of Strength Training*; later Penn State | Hip-flexor range and sprint biomechanics data Moyer cites |
| **Atko Viru** | Endocrine and metabolic adaptation to training; *Adaptation in Sports Training* | Training monitoring |
| **Anatoliy Bondarchuk** | Hammer champion and throws coach; **transfer of training** from correlational data on thousands of athletes | Exercise classification by transfer |
| **Yuri Verkhoshansky** | Shock method (plyometrics), special strength, block training, **dynamic correspondence** and **key movements** | Special-strength exercise design |
| **Nikolai Bernstein** | Degrees-of-freedom problem, variability, **essential vs. non-essential variables** | Motor control, constraints-led coaching |
**Why it works** — Knowing the source tells you the original purpose, population and limits of an idea, so you can tell a genuine advance from a re-labelled old one. Moyer's stronger claim — that modern research (thigh angular velocity, pawback, the two-mass model) **mostly rediscovers Soviet findings** — is his opinion. He supports it with side-by-side slides, not a systematic comparison, and the Soviet papers he relies on (largely *Soviet Sports Review* translations) are hard to check.
**When NOT to apply** — Not a hierarchy of authority. Several biographical details in the lecture are unverified or look wrong (for instance, the claim that Bondarchuk's athletes took every Olympic hammer medal for three Games; see the ingest digest). Soviet work was done in a closed system with limited peer review and state-sponsored doping; it is a source to trace, not a standard to defer to. The table is also Moyer's selection — Western lines (for example Weyand, Clark, Mann) are absent by design.
=== principle--judge-a-sprint-method-by-the-population-it-was-built-on
**What it is** — The one coaching principle worth keeping from Moyer's two hours of Soviet history. The Soviet system **classified athletes by performance standards** (third class up to Master of Sport, with fixed marks such as a 10.3 s 100 m for Master of Sport, as Moyer reads them from a 1981–84 table) and ran both **training and research within a class**. So a Soviet paper would state that its subjects were Class I or Master of Sport athletes. Moyer contrasts this with much Western work "done on 19 recreational athletes, or five soccer players." Two practical halves: **check who a method or study was built on**, and **group your own athletes by physical preparedness**, not by position or talent alone.
**Why it works** — Training responses differ with preparedness: what moves a novice may do nothing for a trained sprinter, and the reverse. Classification gives like-for-like groups, so the training dose and the research result both mean something for the next athlete in that class. The principle is sound. The history behind it is Moyer's narration and is **not verified here**; the Soviet results also rested on state compulsion, a huge talent funnel and pharmacology, which he acknowledges only in part.
**When NOT to apply** — Do not import Soviet classification standards themselves; they were built for track athletes in a different system and era. Do not discard research on recreational subjects outright; for many physiological questions it is the only evidence and may still transfer. And classification by one test (a 40 time) can misgroup athletes whose limits are different; use more than one quality.
=== framework--sprint-technique-analysis-as-qualitative-sequence
**What it is** — Moyer's (and his mentor Michael Yessis's) definition. **Biomechanics** is the physics of movement — numbers, forces, Newton's laws — and on its own "doesn't give us much in the way of practicality": a coach who knows an angle or a force still has to decide what to do. **Technique analysis** combines biomechanics with kinesiology into a **qualitative assessment of three things**: (1) the **key force-producing actions**, (2) the **sequence** in which they happen, and (3) **which muscles do them, where in the range, and how**. The muscle part is what makes it actionable — it names the exercise to train.
**Why it works** — Knowing the sequence and the working muscles lets the analyst go straight from "what is wrong" to "what to train", which a number alone does not do. Moyer's origin story makes the principle concrete: as a high-school strength coach in 2010, he saw his starting quarterback's elbow fracture while throwing a pass with no contact, after a summer of heavy throwing volume. When they sent the boy's throwing film to Yessis, Yessis's first response was that the **sequence was off** and that was why the elbow broke; they then worked on running, cutting and throwing with special strength exercises and technical drills. The usable principle: **when a non-contact injury happens during the skill itself, analyse the skill's sequence, not only the volume.**
**When NOT to apply** — Qualitative sequence analysis is only as good as the analyst's eye and has no reliability data. The quarterback story is a single case told as a conversion experience — Yessis's diagnosis was accepted without any test, and the fracture had an obvious volume cause too. Moyer frames biomechanics as impractical, which undersells it: force plates, GPS and timing data are what confirm whether a qualitative diagnosis changed anything. Use qualitative analysis to generate the hypothesis and measurement to check it.
=== heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint
**What it is** — Moyer's triage rule for any sprint fault that could have a range-of-motion cause. Test the relevant joint **passively** (you move it) and **actively** (the athlete moves it under their own muscle), then branch:
1. **Passive range is lacking** → address the range first (loaded stretches, "time and/or tension"). "First and foremost, they have to have passive. That's number one."
2. **Passive range is adequate but active falls short** (you can lift the thigh high; they cannot) → the gap "should be filled with specific strength exercises": **strength in that range** (PAILs/RAILs, isometrics at end range, special strength exercises).
3. **Both are adequate** → range is not the limiter. It is a strength, coordination or learning issue: technical drills, strength exercises, cues and wearable-load placement ([[framework--sprint-correctives-menu-by-quality]]).
**Why it works** — Passive range tells you whether the tissue and joint *allow* the position. Active range tells you whether the athlete can *produce and control* it. A sprint needs the active version at speed. A drill cannot give range the tissue does not have, and stretching cannot give control the nervous system and muscle cannot produce. The rule matches each deficit to the fix that can plausibly change it. The logic is standard in rehab. Moyer's range-gap training methods come from the FRC/FRS system (see [[heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint]]).
**When NOT to apply** — Reactivity/stiffness faults are usually not range problems. Moyer himself says range "isn't usually going to be a problem" there; it is a strength-quality issue. Range measured on a table is slow and unloaded, so adequate numbers do not guarantee the range is available at sprint speed and fatigue. Moyer gives no validated cut-offs for "adequate" or for an acceptable gap. In the acute phase after injury, a passive–active gap may be protective, and loading end range is a medical decision.

content.text:
I've sent the full review to the agent that launched me. My verdict is GO-WITH-FIXES: the 58 entries match the transcripts closely, and nothing I checked was made up. I made no changes to the vault.

**Coverage:** I opened 37 of the 58 entries, including every case study and all 11 entries from lesson 16. I checked more than 150 numbers, names and quotes against the transcripts. The other 21 entries, mostly `supported` principles and heuristics, I didn't open, so "no confidence mislabels" only covers what I read.

**Must fix:**
1. **College WR splits (lesson 11):** the times are right (1.25→1.15 and 1.73→1.63). Moyer himself says "a 10th off on both his 10 and his 20" (~4:56), so 1.73 is the 20-yd time. The entry should cite that instead of guessing it. His "two tenths" counts the same gain twice. The 10–20 yd split was 0.48 s before and after, so the whole gain came in the first 10 yd. The entry also drops his "wide receiver, I believe."
2. **Natera load table (lesson 16):** the numbers match. Natera does say the 140 and 220 kg push figures exclude body weight. But the entry states that the body-weight benchmarks are total force as fact, when that is inferred from the arithmetic. It needs an inference label.
3. **Najee Harris:** the transcripts do name him. But the library joins him, across three lessons, to a one-sided hamstring history and a failed range test ("Najee was awful"). The course never puts those together in one place. Either de-identify him or Eric decides.
4. **Conflict of interest:** "Moyer sells wearable-resistance coaching" in `_book.md` (repeated in the kinetic-energy entry) isn't in the transcripts. What they do show: he hands out LILA discount codes, uses his own LILA gear, and the course is sponsored by Dasher timing.
5. **NFL running-back case:** it misses that lesson 11 also contradicts lesson 8's "nothing but sprinting and using Lila's," and it overstates the range-test result.

**Other suspects:**
- **"240 fps":** appears only in a made-up Baylor example in the fault-checklist entry. It isn't credited to Moyer, but it isn't labelled as the agent's own number either.
- **Kinetic-energy claim:** clearly marked wrong on units, size and velocity versus acceleration. It cites Moyer's own retraction in Live 3 and is labelled `untested`. No fix needed.
- **Duplicates:** none of the three pairs are true duplicates; each pair splits into two angles on the same idea. The fixes are one-way links to make two-way, and one pair's examples to vary.
- **Confidence labels:** in what I read, no causal, injury or transfer claim is labelled `supported`.

**Validator:** I copied one entry to the tmp folder and corrupted it three ways. My validator (`C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\jobs\afe0ff48\tmp\validate_entries.py`) caught all three: the missing "When NOT to apply", `confidence: proven`, and the dangling `[[no-such-note]]`. I also ran it on the real 58 entries without changing them. It flagged 3 entries with no "Related" section. The ingest-book template doesn't require that section, so these aren't real failures.
